aUSCBBKCOR.meaning: Brave-Butters-Kelley Coincident Index — current economic activity. Real-time GDP-tracking proxy.
aUSCBBKCOR.how_to_use: Tracks GDP contemporaneously. Decelerations precede recession by 0-3 months. Use BBK Leading for forward read, BBK Coincident for current state.

aUSCBBKLER.meaning: Brave-Butters-Kelley Leading Index — a forward-looking activity gauge constructed from a panel of macro indicators. Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.
aUSCBBKLER.how_to_use: Negative readings precede recessions with ~6-12mo lead. Less widely-tracked than the Conference Board LEI but methodologically rigorous. Pair with the BBK Coincident for full picture.

aUSCBBKGPR.meaning: BBK Monthly GDP Growth rate, annualized. Monthly nowcast of GDP — the BBK team's translation of activity data into a GDP-equivalent rate.
aUSCBBKGPR.how_to_use: Compare to Atlanta Fed's GDPNow and NY Fed's Nowcast for consensus on current-quarter GDP. Useful between BEA releases for tracking cycle.

aUSCBBKCYR.description: Brave-Butters-Kelley Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, Cycle component, %
aUSCBBKCYR.meaning: Brave-Butters-Kelley Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, cyclical component — the cyclical-fluctuation portion of the BBK monthly GDP estimate (factor model).
aUSCBBKCYR.how_to_use: Decomposes BBK GDP into trend + cyclical + irregular. The cyclical component is the meaningful business-cycle signal — strips out trend growth and noise. Negative readings precede recessions; positive readings = expansion phase.

aUSCBBKCGR.description: Brave-Butters-Kelley Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, Cycle component, Lagging, %
aUSCBBKCGR.meaning: BBK Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, cyclical-trend component — the trend portion of the cyclical decomposition. Underlying potential-growth pace.
aUSCBBKCGR.how_to_use: Smoother than the cyclical component. Tracks 'trend' GDP growth — currently ~1.8-2.0% reflecting demographic + productivity drivers. Sustained drops below 1.5% suggest secular-stagnation concerns.

aUSCBBKCLR.description: Brave-Butters-Kelley Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, Cycle component, Leading, %
aUSCBBKCLR.meaning: BBK Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, cyclical-cycle component — the pure business-cycle deviation from trend. Negative = below-trend, positive = above-trend.
aUSCBBKCLR.how_to_use: Useful for output-gap estimation. Sustained negative readings = recession-territory output gap. Pair with CBO output gap estimates for triangulated read.

aUSCBBKIRR.description: Brave-Butters-Kelley Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, Irregular component, %
aUSCBBKIRR.meaning: BBK Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, irregular component — the residual noise in the BBK decomposition. Captures one-off shocks not explained by trend or cycle.
aUSCBBKIRR.how_to_use: Spikes during major shocks (2020 COVID, 2008 financial crisis). Used to remove temporary distortions before reading the cyclical signal. Markets typically ignore the irregular component — focus on cyclical.

aUSCBBKTRR.description: Brave-Butters-Kelley Indexes, Monthly GDP Growth, Trend component, %
aUSCBBKTRR.how_to_use: Slow-moving trend. Useful for productivity/labor-supply growth read.

aUSCFNA.description: Chicago Fed CFMMI, National Activity Index
aUSCFNA.meaning: Chicago Fed National Activity Index (CFNAI) — weighted average of 85 monthly indicators (production, employment, sales, consumption). Composite real-time activity gauge.
aUSCFNA.how_to_use: Above 0 = above trend; sustained -0.7 (3-mo avg) signals recession. Most-watched composite activity indicator alongside Conference Board LEI. Released monthly on a 1-month lag.

aUSCFNAAR.description: Chicago Fed National Activity Index - Actual, Index, USD
aUSCFNAAR.meaning: Chicago Fed National Activity Index — alternative release of the same CFNAI data. Captures real-time activity from 85 monthly indicators.
aUSCFNAAR.how_to_use: Cross-check against aUSCFNA. Both are the same CFNAI but at different release vintages. Above-zero = above-trend growth; sustained -0.7 (3-mo MA) signals recession.

aUSNYWER.description: New York Fed, Weekly Economic Index
aUSNYWER.meaning: NY Fed Weekly Economic Index — weekly real GDP-equivalent growth rate. Highest-frequency real-economy gauge.
aUSNYWER.how_to_use: Updated every Tuesday based on 10 weekly indicators. Translates to a quarterly GDP nowcast equivalent. Useful for tracking the cycle between BEA quarterly releases.

aUSKCFSIR.meaning: Kansas City Fed Financial Stress Index.
aUSKCFSIR.how_to_use: Composite financial-conditions gauge. Spikes during 2008, March 2020, March 2023 (regional bank stress).

aUSKCLMCAR.description: Labour Market n.i.e, Kansas City Fed Labor Market Conditions Indicator, Level of Activity
aUSKCLMCAR.meaning: Kansas City Fed Labor Market Conditions Index — composite of 24 labor-market indicators (claims, NFP, hours, wages, JOLTS, household survey). Available in level and momentum forms.
aUSKCLMCAR.how_to_use: Higher-frequency labor-market gauge than the BLS monthly print alone. Sustained negative readings precede labor-market deterioration. Pair with Sahm Rule (aUSRSAHMN/A) and CB ETI (aUSEMPTR) for triangulated cycle call.

aUSKCLMCMR.description: Labour Market n.i.e, Kansas City Fed Labor Market Conditions Indicator, Momentum
aUSKCLMCMR.meaning: KC Fed Labor Market Conditions Index — momentum component (vs level component aUSKCLMCAR). Captures rate-of-change in labor-market conditions.
aUSKCLMCMR.how_to_use: Leading indicator: momentum turns before levels. Negative momentum + positive level = labor market is good but cooling. Watch for sustained negative-momentum readings as recession-leading signal.

aUSSFSIR.description: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, St. Louis Financial Stress Index
aUSSFSIR.meaning: St. Louis Fed Financial Stress Index — composite of 18 weekly financial-market indicators (yields, spreads, vol). Z-score format; zero = normal stress.
aUSSFSIR.how_to_use: Real-time financial-conditions gauge. Spikes during crises (2008 ~6, 2020 ~5, 2023 SVB ~1). Sustained readings >2 indicate market stress beyond normal volatility — Fed often acts when sustained.

aUSSTLFR.description: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, St. Louis Financial Stress Index
aUSSTLFR.meaning: St. Louis Financial Stress Index — alternative release. Same conceptual measure as aUSSFSIR.
aUSSTLFR.how_to_use: Cross-check series. Use whichever has fresher data. Useful for confirming stress regimes — both must agree for confident signal.

aUSSFSIR.1D.description: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, St. Louis Financial Stress Index

aUSNPIRTR/C.how_to_use: Niche real-asset class. Low correlation to stocks/bonds; institutional allocator interest.

aUSSPRPER.description: Standard & Poors, 500 Composite, Cyclically Adjusted Price Earnings Ratio P/E10 or CAPE (Shiller)
aUSSPRPER.meaning: S&P 500 Cyclically Adjusted P/E (Shiller CAPE / P/E10).
aUSSPRPER.how_to_use: Long-run valuation gauge: price / 10-yr inflation-adjusted earnings. >30 historically signals lower forward returns.

aUSSPREPS.description: Standard & Poors, 500 Composite, Index, 12 Month As Reported Earnings per Share (top down)
aUSSPREPS.how_to_use: Earnings denominator for P/E. Compare against operating EPS for accounting-quality drift.

aUSSPMDPS.description: Standard & Poors, 500 Composite, Index, 12 Month Cash Dividends per Share (top down)
aUSSPMDPS.meaning: S&P 500 trailing 12-month dividends per share (index basis) — total cash dividends paid by S&P 500 constituents over the last four quarters, scaled to the index. Updated continuously by S&P Dow Jones Indices.
aUSSPMDPS.how_to_use: Smoother and more cyclical than EPS — companies cut dividends only in extreme stress. Pair with the dividend yield (aUSSPDIVY) for a valuation cross-check, and with EPS to compute the payout ratio. Slow-moving baseline for total-return decomposition.

aUSSPDIVY.description: Standard & Poors, 500 Composite, Index, Dividend Yield
aUSSPDIVY.meaning: S&P 500 dividend yield — index dividends / price.
aUSSPDIVY.how_to_use: Low yields (sub-2%) reflect post-2010 buyback preference. Compare to 10Y Treasury for equity risk premium.

aUSSPCOM.how_to_use: Headline US equity benchmark. Cap-weighted; ~7 megacaps drive much of recent return.

aUSCOINDIF/A.meaning: Conference Board Coincident Economic Index — current-state composite (employment, income, output, sales).
aUSCOINDIF/A.how_to_use: Tracks GDP contemporaneously. Use the LEI/CEI ratio: when LEI growth is below CEI growth for an extended period, recession risk rises.

aUSCOMILNB/A.how_to_use: Business-lending cycle gauge. Slows ahead of recessions; SLOOS tightening leads by 1-2 quarters.

aUSBCIISPI/C.description: Index of stock prices, 500 common stocks
aUSBCIISPI/C.meaning: Index of stock prices, 500 common stocks — embedded in BCI.

aUSEMPIQA.description: Labour Market n.i.e, Employment Trends - Acutal
aUSEMPIQA.meaning: Employment Trends Index — Conference Board, actual.

aUSEMPTR.description: Labour Market n.i.e, The Conference Board Employment Trends Index (ETI)
aUSEMPTR.meaning: Conference Board Employment Trends Index (ETI) — composite of eight labor-market indicators (claims, NFIB hiring plans, jobs hard-to-get, temp employment, hours, ratio of involuntary part-timers, JOLTS hires, employment in manufacturing). Released monthly.
aUSEMPTR.how_to_use: Leads NFP turning points by 2-3 months — historically an excellent labor-market inflection caller. Sustained declines flag rising recession risk before payrolls weaken. Pair with the Sahm Rule for a triangulated read.

aUSLAG/A.meaning: Conference Board Lagging Economic Index — confirmatory, not predictive. Inflation, ULC, prime rate, ratio of consumer credit to income.
aUSLAG/A.how_to_use: Use to confirm cycle turns AFTER the fact. CEI/LAG ratio is itself a leading indicator: lagging components reflect built-up imbalances.

aUSBCILCI/A.meaning: Leading Credit Index — component of LEI.

aUSCLEAD/A.meaning: Conference Board Leading Economic Index (LEI) — composite of 10 leading indicators (yield curve, claims, permits, S&P 500, ISM new orders, etc.).
aUSCLEAD/A.how_to_use: Sustained 6-month declines historically signal recession with 6-12 month lead. False-positive in 2022-23 (predicted recession that didn't materialize as Fed soft-landed). Use alongside yield curve, not in isolation.

aUSLIDXIR10.description: Leading Index, Interest rate spread, 10-year Treasury bonds less federal funds
aUSLIDXIR10.meaning: 10Y Treasury minus fed funds rate — recession-warning yield-curve spread.
aUSLIDXIR10.how_to_use: Inverted curve (negative spread) has preceded every US recession since 1970. Watch slope dynamics, not just sign.

aUSLI500CH/C.description: Leading Index, Stock prices, 500 common stocks
aUSLI500CH/C.meaning: Stock prices, 500 common stocks — LEI component.

aUSLEADAR.description: Leading index chg- Actual, Chg P/P
aUSLEADAR.how_to_use: Most market-moving LEI series at release. -0.3% MoM consensus is the threshold for hawk/dove read.

aUSSTOPUKR/C.meaning: UK stock prices — included for cross-country reference.

aUSCARSOA.how_to_use: Cars dropped from ~50% to ~25% of light-vehicle sales since 2010. EV adoption is reshaping the car segment specifically (Tesla, Rivian, Lucid). Truck SAAR (aUSVHLS − aUSCARSOA) is the larger and more cyclical segment.

aUSATSOA.how_to_use: Trucks = ~75% of light-vehicle sales now (CUV + pickup mix shift).

aUSAUIMCNO/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Auto unit imports, Canada
aUSAUIMCNO/A.meaning: Auto unit imports from Canada — passenger vehicles imported from Canadian plants. Canada is integrated with US auto manufacturing under USMCA.
aUSAUIMCNO/A.how_to_use: Track for USMCA trade flows. Canadian plants produce primarily for US export (Honda Alliston, Toyota Cambridge, GM Oshawa). Tariff threats (2018, 2025) directly impact this series.

aUSDCAR.description: Motor Vehicles, Car sales, domestic passenger
aUSDCAR.meaning: Domestic passenger car sales — cars assembled in US/Canada/Mexico (USMCA). Excludes vehicles imported from Asia or Europe.
aUSDCAR.how_to_use: Track domestic vs imported share for trade-policy implications. Tariff regime changes show up here first. Domestic share has fallen as Asian OEMs shifted to US assembly (Toyota, Honda, Hyundai, Kia all have major US plants).

aUSDVEHCAR/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Car sales, domestic passenger
aUSDVEHCAR/A.meaning: Domestic passenger car sales — annual aggregate of cars assembled in USMCA region. Companion to aUSDCAR at lower frequency.
aUSDVEHCAR/A.how_to_use: Use for long-term-trend analysis of domestic-vs-imported auto mix. Domestic car share has fallen as Asian OEMs shifted to US assembly (Toyota, Honda, Hyundai, Kia all have major US plants).

aUSIMPMV/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Car sales, imported passenger
aUSIMPMV/A.meaning: Imported passenger car sales (annual) — vehicles imported from outside USMCA region. Companion to aUSICAR at lower frequency. Mostly European luxury and Japanese/Korean supplements.
aUSIMPMV/A.how_to_use: Sensitive to tariff policy and currency moves. Watch USDJPY and EURUSD for currency-pass-through. Section-232 tariff threats specifically target this category.

aUSICAR.description: Motor Vehicles, Car sales, imported passenger
aUSICAR.meaning: Imported passenger car sales — vehicles imported from outside USMCA region. Mostly European (German luxury, UK premium) plus some Korean and Japanese supplements to US production.
aUSICAR.how_to_use: Sensitive to tariff policy and currency moves. EU tariff changes (proposed 2018-19, 2025) directly hit this series. Watch USDJPY and EURUSD for currency-pass-through to import-vehicle prices.

aUSNCAR.meaning: Total car sales (passenger sedans, hatchbacks, sports cars — excluding light trucks/SUVs). Has structurally declined post-2010 as US shifted to SUV/CUV preference.
aUSNCAR.how_to_use: Cars are now ~25% of light-vehicle sales (was 50% in 2010). Track separately from trucks for demand-mix signal. EVs are mostly classified as cars in this data; rapid EV growth partially offsets ICE-car decline.

aUSNCAR/A.meaning: Total car sales (annual) — sum of domestic + imported passenger cars. Companion to aUSNCAR at lower frequency.
aUSNCAR/A.how_to_use: Annual frequency cleaner for trend analysis. Cars now ~25% of US light-vehicle market (was 50% in 2010). EVs included as cars in this data; track separately for EV-specific share.

aUSPCARRVO/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Domestic auto unit inventory
aUSPCARRVO/A.meaning: Domestic auto unit inventory — outstanding stock of unsold vehicles at dealer + manufacturer level. Days-supply ratio (inventory/daily sales rate) is the cleaner stress signal.
aUSPCARRVO/A.how_to_use: Pre-COVID norm ~60-90 days supply for cars, ~80-100 for trucks. 2022 supply shock saw <30 days; rebuilding now toward normal. Watch for inventory build above 100 days as a sign of demand softening.

aUSPCARRVP.description: Motor Vehicles, Domestic auto unit inventory, inventory level (Ward's)
aUSPCARRVP.meaning: Domestic auto unit inventory levels — alternative measure to aUSPCARRVO/A. Same underlying inventory concept at different frequency/release.
aUSPCARRVP.how_to_use: Cross-check against aUSPCARRVO/A. Days-supply ratio (inventory/daily sales) is the meaningful stress signal — under 30 days = tight, over 100 = loose. Watch alongside production for the inventory-build-or-draw signal.

aUSDAPRODP.description: Motor Vehicles, Domestic auto unit production
aUSDAPRODP.meaning: Domestic auto unit production — vehicles assembled in US plants. Companion to sales for the supply-side picture.
aUSDAPRODP.how_to_use: Inventories = production minus sales over time. Track for supply-discipline signal: when production exceeds sales, inventories build and OEM incentives rise. Chip-shortage 2021-22 caused production crater while demand persisted, driving used-car prices and CPI.

aUSTSALE/CA.description: Motor Vehicles, Total light trucks sales
aUSTSALE/CA.meaning: Total light truck sales (SUVs + pickups + minivans). ~75% of US light-vehicle market. Higher-margin segment for OEMs.
aUSTSALE/CA.how_to_use: Pickup truck demand correlates with construction and small-business activity (most pickups go to commercial buyers). Pickup-vs-SUV split useful for B2B vs consumer breakdown. Larger segment sees biggest dealer-incentive moves.

aUSTKLSAP.description: Motor Vehicles, Total light trucks sales
aUSTKLSAP.meaning: Total light truck sales (alternative source) — same conceptual measure as aUSTSALE/CA at different release vintage.
aUSTKLSAP.how_to_use: Cross-check against aUSTSALE/CA. Use whichever has fresher data. Light truck mix is the structural story of US auto market: from 30% of mix in 1990 to 75% today.

aUSDVEHLCV/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Total light vehicle sales
aUSDVEHLCV/A.meaning: Total light vehicle sales (annualized) — companion series to aUSVHLS at quarterly/annual frequency. Same conceptual measure for long-time-series comparison.
aUSDVEHLCV/A.how_to_use: Cross-check against aUSVHLS. Use the higher-frequency series for monthly tracking. Long-term trend has shifted from cars (sedan-dominated 1990s) to trucks/SUVs (~75% of mix today).

aUSVHLS.description: Motor Vehicles, Total light vehicle sales
aUSVHLS.meaning: Total light-vehicle sales (cars + light trucks) at seasonally-adjusted annual rate. Released monthly (Wards Auto / Autodata).
aUSVHLS.how_to_use: The headline US auto-sales print. Pre-COVID norm ~17M SAAR; supply-chain shock dropped to 13M in 2021-22; recovering toward 16M. Major demand input to GDP (consumer durables) and to inflation (used-car CPI is auto-sales-volume driven).

aUSTKHSALO/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Truck Sales, Heavy trucks sales
aUSTKHSALO/A.how_to_use: Class 8 trucks — freight-cycle indicator. Order books lead by 6-9 months.

aUSTKHSAO/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Truck Sales, Heavy trucks sales
aUSTKHSAO/A.meaning: Heavy truck (Class 8) sales — semi-tractors, cement mixers, dump trucks. Sold mostly to fleet operators and trucking companies. ~250-450k units/year.
aUSTKHSAO/A.how_to_use: Pure cyclical indicator: trucking demand → fleet replacement → orders. Sustained drops below 350k SAAR have preceded freight recessions. ATA's truck tonnage index is the demand-side companion.

aUSTKHSAP.description: Motor Vehicles, Truck Sales, Heavy trucks sales
aUSTKHSAP.meaning: Heavy truck (Class 8) sales — alternative source. Cross-check with aUSTKHSAO/A. Pure cyclical indicator: trucking demand → fleet replacement → orders.
aUSTKHSAP.how_to_use: Use whichever is fresher. Sustained drops below 350k SAAR have preceded freight recessions. ATA's truck tonnage index is the demand-side companion.

aUSMVEHTRKL.description: Motor Vehicles, Truck sales, domestic light
aUSMVEHTRKL.meaning: Domestic light truck sales — companion to aUSDTRUCK/A. Captures pickups + SUVs assembled in US/Canada/Mexico under USMCA.
aUSMVEHTRKL.how_to_use: Watch for nearshoring effects. Production has shifted from Mexico for some models, expanding US assembly. Track alongside aUSMVTSIMPL for full domestic-vs-imported truck mix.

aUSDTRUCK/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Truck sales, domestic light
aUSDTRUCK/A.meaning: Domestic light truck sales (annual aggregate) — companion to monthly truck sales at lower frequency. USMCA-region production.
aUSDTRUCK/A.how_to_use: Use for long-term-trend analysis. Domestic-vs-imported share key for trade-policy implications. Pickup trucks dominate this category.

aUSMVTSIMPL/A.description: Motor Vehicles, Truck sales, imported light
aUSMVTSIMPL/A.meaning: Imported light truck sales (annual) — non-USMCA-sourced light trucks. Mostly Asian and European origin.
aUSMVTSIMPL/A.how_to_use: Smaller share than imported cars because tariffs on imported pickups (25%, 'chicken tax') have historically protected US pickup makers. Subject to tariff-policy risk.

aUSTSLSIMPL.description: Motor Vehicles, Truck sales, imported light
aUSTSLSIMPL.meaning: Imported light truck sales (alternate source) — same conceptual measure as aUSMVTSIMPL/A.
aUSTSLSIMPL.how_to_use: Cross-check series. Use whichever is fresher. Tariff-protected category historically.

aUSSRAMDAO.description: AUTODATA RETAIL SALES OF NEW CARS: DOMESTIC (AR)
aUSSRAMDAO.meaning: Autodata Retail Sales of New Cars: Domestic (Annualized Rate) — Autodata Corp's measure of domestic-only car sales (USMCA-assembled passenger cars only).
aUSSRAMDAO.how_to_use: Track for domestic-vs-import retail mix. Autodata is a primary source automakers report through; J.D. Power and Wards aggregate their data.

aUSTLVS.description: Motor Vehicles, Total light vehicle sales (Autodata Corp.)
aUSTLVS.meaning: Total light vehicle sales (Autodata Corp) — alternative provider's measure of the same total light-vehicle sales. Useful for cross-check when source data revisions diverge.
aUSTLVS.how_to_use: Autodata is the source most automakers report through. Compare against Wards Auto-sourced series to see methodology differences. Major divergences are usually corrected within 1-2 months.

aUSDCAAO.description: United States, REUTERS POLL: DOMESTIC CAR SALES - ACTUAL, Volume, Automobiles & Transport, Monthly, Reuters
aUSDCAAO.meaning: Reuters Poll: Domestic Car Sales — Actual — Reuters survey-based estimate of monthly domestic car sales, used pre-release as forecast benchmark.
aUSDCAAO.how_to_use: Used by markets to anchor expectations before official release. Comparison vs actual print drives short-term auto-sector trades.

aUSDTRAO.description: United States, REUTERS POLL: DOMESTIC TRUCK SALES - ACTUAL, Volume, Automobiles & Transport, Monthly, Reuters
aUSDTRAO.meaning: Reuters Poll: Domestic Truck Sales — Actual — Reuters poll-based estimate. Markets use as forecast benchmark before official monthly release.
aUSDTRAO.how_to_use: Survey-anchored estimate. Comparison vs actual print drives auto-sector reaction. Domestic truck sales matter for domestic-OEM share (Ford F-150, Chevy Silverado, Ram).

aUSVEHAO.description: United States, REUTERS POLL: TOTAL VEHICLE SALES - ACTUAL, Volume, Automobiles & Transport, Monthly, Reuters
aUSVEHAO.meaning: Reuters Poll: Total Vehicle Sales — Actual — Reuters total-vehicle-sales survey estimate, anchor for monthly release expectations.
aUSVEHAO.how_to_use: Most-watched of the Reuters auto polls. Comparison vs actual print drives broad auto-sector trades. ~17M SAAR = healthy; <14M = stressed.

aUSACAV.description: Air Cargo Traffic, Available Ton Miles
aUSACAV.how_to_use: Cargo capacity. Spread to revenue ton-miles = utilization (load factor).

aUSACRFRM.description: Air Cargo Traffic, Revenue Freight Ton Miles
aUSACRFRM.meaning: Air cargo traffic, revenue freight ton-miles — total air freight activity at US airports. BTS monthly release.
aUSACRFRM.how_to_use: Cyclical: tracks goods trade and e-commerce demand. Spiked 2020-21 during pandemic e-commerce surge. Watch alongside trucking and rail freight for full freight-cycle picture.

aUSBSSMILP.description: Air Passenger Traffic, Available Seat Miles
aUSBSSMILP.how_to_use: Industry capacity. Pairs with passenger miles for load factor.

aUSPTRAH.description: Air Passenger Traffic, Revenue Aircraft Hours (Airborne)
aUSPTRAH.meaning: Air passenger traffic, revenue aircraft hours (airborne). BTS monthly. Captures fleet-utilization for passenger flights.
aUSPTRAH.how_to_use: Tracks passenger-flight activity. Recovered fully from COVID by 2024. Watch for capacity discipline post-recovery (airlines avoiding overcapacity).

aUSPTRAMF.description: Air Passenger Traffic, Revenue Aircraft Miles Flown
aUSPTRAMF.meaning: Air passenger traffic, revenue aircraft miles flown — total miles flown by passenger aircraft. Companion to aircraft-hours.
aUSPTRAMF.how_to_use: Tracks long-haul vs short-haul mix. Long-haul international has lagged domestic in COVID recovery. Watch alongside aircraft-hours for trip-length signal.

aUSPTRDEP.description: Air Passenger Traffic, Revenue Departures Performed
aUSPTRDEP.meaning: Air passenger traffic, revenue departures performed — number of passenger flights operated.
aUSPTRDEP.how_to_use: Tracks total flight count. Combined with passenger enplanements gives load-factor implications. Departure count is more frequency-driven; enplanements more demand-driven.

aUSPTRPEP.description: Air Passenger Traffic, Revenue Passenger Enplanements
aUSPTRPEP.meaning: Air passenger traffic, revenue passenger enplanements — total passengers boarding flights. The 'how many people flew' number.
aUSPTRPEP.how_to_use: Cyclical with leisure + business travel demand. TSA security throughput is the high-frequency complement. Watch for peak-summer-travel season trends and post-COVID business-travel recovery.

aUSAIRP.description: Air Passenger Traffic, Revenue Passenger Miles, U.S. carriers
aUSAIRP.how_to_use: Combines headcount with stage length. The headline air-travel demand metric.

aUSACTOT.description: Air Passenger Traffic, Total Revenue Ton Miles
aUSACTOT.meaning: Air passenger traffic, total revenue ton-miles — combined passenger + cargo ton-miles. Captures total revenue-generating activity.
aUSACTOT.how_to_use: Aggregate aviation activity gauge. Watch for overall airline industry health. Decompose into passenger vs cargo for source of growth/weakness.

aUSTRANSF/A.how_to_use: BTS combined freight gauge: trucking, rail, water, pipeline, air freight. Leads industrial production.

aUSTRANSP/A.meaning: Transportation Services Index, passenger — BTS composite of passenger transportation activity (air, rail, transit). Released monthly.
aUSTRANSP/A.how_to_use: Real-time passenger-transportation pulse. Combined with freight-side TSI gives total-transportation cycle gauge. Useful as a coincident-economy indicator.

aUSTRANS/A.how_to_use: BTS combined transport activity (passenger + freight). Leading indicator.

aUSCAPAC/A.how_to_use: Tiny line — debt forgiveness, capital transfers. Mostly rounding error.

aUSCURAC.meaning: US Current Account balance — total. Sum of trade in goods + services, primary income (investment income), and secondary income (transfers). BEA quarterly.
aUSCURAC.how_to_use: Persistently negative ~$200-300B/quarter. Funded by capital inflows (financial account = mirror image, BoP identity). >5% of GDP deficit historically signals stress; current ~3% is sustainable for a reserve currency.

aUSGS/A.meaning: Goods trade balance (exports of goods minus imports of goods) on a balance-of-payments basis. The largest component of the US current account deficit, persistently negative for ~50 years.
aUSGS/A.how_to_use: Watch monthly trade-balance prints (Census/BEA International Trade Report) for the high-frequency read. Petroleum component swings with oil prices; non-petroleum is the structural import dependence on consumer goods + capital goods. Tariff regime changes show up here first.

aUSCUBAL/A.how_to_use: Trade balance excluding income flows. Goods deficit + services surplus.

aUSBALFAT/A.description: Balance, Net Lending or Borrowing from Financial Account Transactions
aUSBALFAT/A.meaning: Net Lending/Borrowing from Financial Account — accounting mirror of the current account. Equal in magnitude (and opposite in sign) to the CA balance by construction.
aUSBALFAT/A.how_to_use: Useful for cross-check on CA data; if they don't match exactly, the residual is 'statistical discrepancy'. Big discrepancies (>$50B) suggest measurement error in trade or financial data.

aUSCUIV/A.meaning: Primary income balance — net investment income from abroad.
aUSCUIV/A.how_to_use: US owns large foreign assets — earns income. Declining surplus as foreign holdings of US grow.

aUSCURACTRN/A.meaning: Current Account: secondary income balance — net transfers including remittances, foreign aid, government grants. Consistently negative for the US (large remittance outflows + foreign aid > inflows).
aUSCURACTRN/A.how_to_use: Small relative to goods/services balance (-$150B vs -$1T goods). Useful for understanding why total CA differs from trade balance. Less market-relevant — analysts focus on goods/services and primary income.

aUSCUSERV/A.how_to_use: Persistent surplus. Financial, IP licensing, travel, business services.

aUSCURAAB.meaning: Current Account, Balance — the broad external balance combining goods, services, primary income, and secondary income flows. Same construct as aUSCURAC/A but at a different frequency/release.
aUSCURAAB.how_to_use: Cross-check against aUSCURAC/A. The US has run a persistent CA deficit since the early 1980s; financed by capital inflows. Useful for reading external imbalances when paired with the trade balance and FDI flows.

aUSCURAC/A.meaning: US Current Account balance — the broadest external balance, summing the goods balance, services balance, primary income (investment income on foreign assets), and secondary income (transfers). Released quarterly by BEA.
aUSCURAC/A.how_to_use: Persistently negative ($800B-$1T deficit annually post-2020). Compare to GDP — sustained deficits >5% of GDP have historically preceded currency stress, but the dollar's reserve status has insulated the US. Watch alongside the financial account (mirror image by accounting identity).

aUSCURACCGS/A.description: Current Account, Exports of Goods and Services and Income Receipts
aUSCURACCGS/A.meaning: Current Account: total exports of goods, services, and primary income — the inflows side of the broader CA. Sums goods exports + services exports + primary-income receipts.
aUSCURACCGS/A.how_to_use: Total credit side of the CA. Compare against aUSCURACDGS/A (debits) to see net flows. Useful for understanding why goods deficit is offset by services + primary-income surpluses.

aUSCURACEXG/A.meaning: Current Account: goods exports — same as aUSCEXBA in the broader CA framing. The largest export category; the services surplus is what offsets goods deficits in the broader CA.
aUSCURACEXG/A.how_to_use: Track YoY growth as a global-demand proxy. Volume vs price decomposition useful: nominal export growth of 5% with import-price inflation of 3% means real export volume growth of ~2%.

aUSCURACEXS/A.meaning: Current Account: services exports — financial services, intellectual-property royalties, business services, travel and transport. The persistent US surplus driver that partially offsets goods deficits.
aUSCURACEXS/A.how_to_use: Travel is the most cyclical (tourism). IP royalties are the most structural (US tech and pharma dominance). Services balance has been ~$200-300B surplus pre-COVID; declined during pandemic; recovering since.

aUSCURACDGS/A.description: Current Account, Imports of Goods and Services and Income Payments
aUSCURACDGS/A.meaning: Current Account: total imports of goods, services, and primary income — the outflows side of the broader CA. Sums goods imports + services imports + primary-income payments.
aUSCURACDGS/A.how_to_use: Total debit side of the CA. Larger than CCGS/A in any deficit year. Decompose to find where the deficit comes from: goods (largest), services (small surplus offsetting), or primary income (becoming smaller surplus as foreign claims on US grow).

aUSCURACIMG/A.meaning: Current Account: goods imports — same as aUSCIMBA in the broader CA framing. Largest import category, driven by consumer + capital goods.
aUSCURACIMG/A.how_to_use: Cyclical with consumer demand. Watch tariff impacts: post-2018 imports from China fell while imports from Vietnam, Mexico rose (trade diversion, not reduction). Structural shift to nearshoring is visible in bilateral data.

aUSCURACIMS/A.meaning: Current Account: services imports — US payments to foreigners for travel, transport, business services, royalties. Smaller than services exports — US is a net services exporter.
aUSCURACIMS/A.how_to_use: Travel imports (US residents traveling abroad) is the largest and most cyclical component. Watch for outbound tourism surges as a sign of strong household balance sheets.

aUSFINACF/A.description: Financial Account, Net US Incurrence of Liabilities Excluding Financial Derivatives
aUSFINACF/A.meaning: Financial Account: net US incurrence of liabilities — foreign claims on US (capital inflows). The accounting mirror of the current account: the US runs CA deficits financed by selling assets (Treasuries, equities, real estate) to foreigners.
aUSFINACF/A.how_to_use: When inflows slow, dollar weakens or Treasury yields rise. Foreign Treasury holdings (TIC data, separate series) are the most-watched component. Recent shifts: official-sector Asian buying down, private-sector European buying up.

aUSIVDFA.description: Investment, Capital, Foreign direct investment in the U.S. Total
aUSIVDFA.meaning: Foreign direct investment IN the US — total.
aUSIVDFA.how_to_use: Inward FDI. ~$5T cumulative stock. UK, Japan, Netherlands largest sources.

aUSIVDFAUA.description: Investment, Capital, Foreign direct investment in the U.S., Australia
aUSIVDFAUA.meaning: Foreign direct investment in US from Australia — cumulative stock. Smaller bilateral relationship; mostly mining, financial services, real estate.
aUSIVDFAUA.how_to_use: Track for AUD-USD investment flows. Australian super funds (largest pension pool) have grown US allocations significantly post-2010. Less cyclical than European or Asian inward FDI.

aUSIVDFCNA.description: Investment, Capital, Foreign direct investment in the U.S., Canada
aUSIVDFCNA.meaning: Foreign direct investment in US from Canada — cumulative stock. Major bilateral; Canadian banks (TD, RBC, BMO), pension funds (CPP, OTPP, CDPQ), energy infrastructure, retail.
aUSIVDFCNA.how_to_use: Largest inward FDI source historically due to North American economic integration. Canadian pension funds are major US infrastructure and real-estate investors. Track alongside outward FDI to Canada (aUSIVDACNA) for the bilateral.

aUSIVDFBDA.description: Investment, Capital, Foreign direct investment in the U.S., Germany
aUSIVDFBDA.meaning: Foreign direct investment in US from Germany — cumulative stock. Top-5 source, dominated by auto manufacturing (BMW, Mercedes, VW), chemicals, and industrial machinery.
aUSIVDFBDA.how_to_use: Watch for reshoring/IRA-driven investments: German auto and chemicals firms have announced major US plants 2022-25 in response to Inflation Reduction Act subsidies and tariff risk.

aUSIVDFJPA.description: Investment, Capital, Foreign direct investment in the U.S., Japan
aUSIVDFJPA.meaning: Foreign direct investment in US from Japan — cumulative stock. Top-3 source: auto manufacturing (Toyota, Honda, Nissan, Subaru), financial services, real estate.
aUSIVDFJPA.how_to_use: Major bilateral — Japan invested heavily in US auto manufacturing post-1980s to circumvent voluntary export restraints. Now Japanese OEMs produce ~60% of their US sales domestically. Track yen carry-trade and Japan corporate buybacks for inflow flows.

aUSIVDFUKA.description: Investment, Capital, Foreign direct investment in the U.S., United Kingdom
aUSIVDFUKA.how_to_use: Largest single bilateral source. Financial + media + pharma.

aUSIVDAAUA.description: Investment, Capital, U.S. direct investment abroad, Australia
aUSIVDAAUA.meaning: US direct investment in Australia — cumulative stock. Smaller bilateral; mostly mining (energy + minerals), financial services, retail.
aUSIVDAAUA.how_to_use: Resource-sector heavy. Track for commodity-cycle exposure: US miners (Newmont, Freeport) have major AU operations. Less cyclical than European destinations because of mining-asset stickiness.

aUSIVDACNA.description: Investment, Capital, U.S. direct investment abroad, Canada
aUSIVDACNA.meaning: US direct investment in Canada — cumulative stock. Major bilateral due to integrated North American manufacturing. Auto + energy + financial services dominated.
aUSIVDACNA.how_to_use: Auto OEMs (Big 3) have deep Canadian operations under USMCA. Energy: pipelines (Enbridge, TC Energy), oil sands (ExxonMobil, ConocoPhillips). Track for tariff/USMCA renegotiation impact.

aUSIVDABDA.description: Investment, Capital, U.S. direct investment abroad, Germany
aUSIVDABDA.meaning: US direct investment in Germany — cumulative stock. Large bilateral; auto components (manufacturing supply chains for VW, BMW, Mercedes), chemicals, business services.
aUSIVDABDA.how_to_use: Pharmaceutical and tech-services heavy. Track for tax-driven repatriation effects. Germany's chemicals sector deeply integrated with US: BASF, Bayer, Henkel are major US operators; Dow, DuPont, ExxonMobil have major German sites.

aUSIVDAMXA.description: Investment, Capital, U.S. direct investment abroad, Mexico
aUSIVDAMXA.meaning: US direct investment in Mexico — cumulative stock. Heavy in manufacturing under USMCA — autos, electronics, appliances. Has accelerated post-2018 with nearshoring trend.
aUSIVDAMXA.how_to_use: A canary for nearshoring/friend-shoring policy effects. Auto OEMs and electronics manufacturers have been moving production from China to Mexico since 2018. Compare growth rate to direct investment in China for the rebalancing signal.

aUSIVDAUKA.description: Investment, Capital, U.S. direct investment abroad, United Kingdom
aUSIVDAUKA.meaning: US direct investment in UK — cumulative stock. Largest single European bilateral. Financial services + business services + manufacturing. ~$900B+ position.
aUSIVDAUKA.how_to_use: London is the European HQ for many US multinationals (JPM, Goldman, Citi, BAML, McKinsey). Track for Brexit effects (some flows shifted to Frankfurt, Paris, Dublin) and for tax-policy changes (UK corporate tax raised 2023).

aUSIVDAA.description: Investment, Capital, U.S. direct investment abroad, total
aUSIVDAA.meaning: US Direct Investment Abroad (outward FDI position) — cumulative stock of US-owned subsidiaries and majority stakes in foreign companies. ~$6T position, larger than inward FDI.
aUSIVDAA.how_to_use: Track as a long-term indicator of US corporate global footprint. UK, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Canada, Ireland are top destinations (often as holding-company hubs). Used to gauge dollar repatriation potential under tax-policy changes.

aUSCAFBAL/A.description: United States, CAPITAL AND FINANCIAL ACCOUNT BALANCE, Current Prices, Balance of Payments, Quarterly, BEA - Bureau of Economic Analysis, U.S. Department of Commerce
aUSCAFBAL/A.meaning: Capital and financial account balance, current prices.

aUSCCURQ/A.description: Current Account Balance as a percentage of GDP, Standardized
aUSCCURQ/A.meaning: Current account balance as % of GDP, standardized.
aUSCCURQ/A.how_to_use: Sustainability gauge. ~3% deficit normal for reserve currency. >5% historical warning.

aUSCCURPQ/A.description: Current Account Balance as a percentage of GDP, quarter on quarter, Standardized

aUSCCURYQ/A.description: Current Account Balance as a percentage of GDP, year on year, Standardized

aUSCCURPB/A.description: Current Account Balance, quarter on quarter, Standardized, Absolute change

aUSCCURYB/A.description: Current Account Balance, year on year, Standardized, Absolute change

aUSCEXBPA.description: Exports of Goods, Balance of Payments Basis, % month on month, Standardized, Chg P/P
aUSCEXBPA.meaning: Exports of goods, BoP basis, standardized MoM%.

aUSCEXBYA.description: Exports of Goods, Balance of Payments Basis, % year on year, Standardized, Chg Y/Y
aUSCEXBYA.meaning: Exports of goods, BoP basis, YoY%.

aUSCEXBA.description: Exports of Goods, Balance of Payments Basis, Standardized
aUSCEXBA.meaning: US goods exports on BoP basis — total value of merchandise sold abroad. Driven by capital goods, industrial supplies, autos, agricultural, and consumer goods.
aUSCEXBA.how_to_use: Pair with aUSCIMBA (imports) to get the trade balance. Sensitive to global growth (export volumes) and the dollar (price competitiveness). Falls early in global slowdowns — a leading global-cycle indicator.

aUSCIMBPA.description: Imports of Goods, Balance of Payments Basis, % month on month, Standardized, Chg P/P
aUSCIMBPA.meaning: Imports of goods, BoP basis, standardized MoM%.

aUSCIMBYA.description: Imports of Goods, Balance of Payments Basis, % year on year, Standardized, Chg Y/Y
aUSCIMBYA.meaning: Imports of goods, BoP basis, YoY%.

aUSCIMBA.description: Imports of Goods, Balance of Payments Basis, Standardized
aUSCIMBA.meaning: US goods imports on BoP basis — total value of foreign merchandise purchased. Dominated by consumer goods, capital goods, industrial supplies, autos, and petroleum.
aUSCIMBA.how_to_use: Cyclical with US consumption — falls in recessions when goods demand slows. Petroleum imports have shrunk dramatically post-shale (US is now near-balanced in energy). Consumer goods imports track retail sales closely.

aUSCBOPA.description: Visible Trade Balance, Balance of Payments Basis, Standardized
aUSCBOPA.meaning: Visible (goods-only) trade balance on BoP basis — same conceptual measure as aUSGS/A in different framing. Goods exports minus goods imports excluding services.
aUSCBOPA.how_to_use: The 'big number' in monthly trade reports. Markets parse the petroleum vs non-petroleum split to gauge structural vs cyclical movement. China and Mexico are the largest bilateral deficits; tariff policy moves these first.

aUSCBOPPA.description: Visible Trade Balance, Balance of Payments Basis, month on month, Standardized, Absolute change
aUSCBOPPA.meaning: Visible trade balance, MoM absolute change.

aUSCBOPYA.description: Visible Trade Balance, Balance of Payments Basis, year on year, Standardized, Absolute change
aUSCBOPYA.meaning: Visible trade balance, YoY absolute change.

aUSBNKQPTP.description: Bankruptcy filings (3 months ending), business, total
aUSBNKQPTP.meaning: Business bankruptcy filings, 3-month rolling. From AOUSC.
aUSBNKQPTP.how_to_use: Trailing indicator. Spikes during recessions. Watch alongside delinquency rates and tightening lending standards.

aUSBNQNP.description: Bankruptcy filings (3 months ending), non-business, total
aUSBNQNP.how_to_use: Rises with consumer debt distress. Healthcare costs and divorce historically the dominant drivers.

aUSBNRQP.meaning: Total US bankruptcy filings — sum of business and non-business (consumer) Chapter 7, 11, and 13 filings. Released quarterly by the Administrative Office of the US Courts.
aUSBNRQP.how_to_use: Cyclical late-cycle stress signal. Spikes when consumer credit delinquencies and business defaults pick up — typically lags labor weakness by 6-9 months. The 2005 BAPCPA reform created a structural break; pre-2005 levels not directly comparable to post-2005.

aUSCBAITX.meaning: Commercial Banks: Applicable income taxes — federal + state taxes paid by US commercial banks. FDIC quarterly Call Report.
aUSCBAITX.how_to_use: Tracks bank profitability after tax. Useful for ROE calculations and post-tax-reform impact analysis (2017 TCJA cut bank effective tax rates from ~28% to ~21%). Bank earnings trends visible here lag pretax income.

aUSCBININ.how_to_use: Surged 2022-23 with rate hikes. Watch alongside interest expense for NIM trend.

aUSCBINXP.how_to_use: Lagged the rate cycle (deposit betas). Compresses NIM when finally repricing.

aUSCBNINC.how_to_use: Aggregate banking system bottom line. Highly cyclical; watch ROE/ROA for normalized health.

aUSCBNIIN.how_to_use: Core banking earnings = interest income − interest expense. The biggest swing factor in bank profitability.

aUSCBNIEX.meaning: Commercial banks, non-interest expense (compensation, occupancy, tech, etc).
aUSCBNIEX.how_to_use: Efficiency ratio (non-int exp / revenue) is a key metric. ~55-60% is healthy for large banks.

aUSCBNIIC.meaning: Commercial banks, non-interest income (fees, trading, mortgage banking, advisory).
aUSCBNIIC.how_to_use: More volatile than NII. Helps diversify earnings; surged with capital markets activity.

aUSCBNINS.how_to_use: Long-term decline (4,500+ in 2010 to ~4,000 today) from M&A and failures. Concentration is rising.

aUSCBPTNO.description: Commercial banks, pre-tax net operating income
aUSCBPTNO.meaning: Commercial banks, pre-tax net operating income.
aUSCBPTNO.how_to_use: Strips out tax effects. Cleaner operating-performance read than after-tax net income.

aUSCBPLLL.description: Commercial banks, provision for loan & lease losses
aUSCBPLLL.meaning: Commercial banks, provision for loan and lease losses.
aUSCBPLLL.how_to_use: Counter-cyclical: rises sharply going into recessions. CECL accounting now front-loads provisions.

aUSCBSGLO.how_to_use: Realized gains/losses on bond holdings. Big losses in 2022 from rising rates (HTM avoided realization).

aUSBCACIB/A.description: Assets and liab of cml banks, commercial & industrial
aUSBCACIB/A.meaning: Commercial and Industrial loans outstanding at commercial banks (Fed H.8). Business credit cycle gauge.
aUSBCACIB/A.how_to_use: Slows ahead of recessions; SLOOS lending standards typically lead loan-volume slowdowns by 1-2 quarters. Currently flat-ish — banks tightened standards 2023-24 in response to deposit competition + CRE worries.

aUSBCALCB.description: Assets and liab of cml banks, consumer
aUSBCALCB.meaning: Consumer loans outstanding at commercial banks — credit cards + auto + other consumer (excluding real estate). Different from aUSCRDOUTA (G.19) which captures ALL consumer credit issuers.
aUSBCALCB.how_to_use: Banks are ~50% of the consumer credit market. Watch alongside G.19 total to gauge shadow-bank vs bank shifts. Credit unions + finance companies + securitization pools complete the picture.

aUSBCAOLLB/A.description: Assets and liab of cml banks, other loans and leases
aUSBCAOLLB/A.meaning: Commercial Banks: Other loans and leases — non-traditional lending categories (lease financing, acceptances, agricultural production loans).
aUSBCAOLLB/A.how_to_use: Smaller than C&I, real estate, or consumer loan books. Useful for tracking lease-finance trends (declining as direct lending replaces leasing) and for full bank-credit picture.

aUSBCAREB/A.description: Assets and liab of cml banks, real estate
aUSBCAREB/A.meaning: Real Estate loans outstanding at commercial banks — residential mortgages + CRE. Largest single bank loan category.
aUSBCAREB/A.how_to_use: CRE stress concentrated in regional banks (large banks cleaner). Office sector weighs on aggregate; multifamily + industrial healthier. Watch SLOOS for CRE tightening signals.

aUSZQDIBP.description: IFDI, Financial Performance Indicator, Islamic Banking, Full Fledged Banks
aUSZQDIBP.meaning: IFDI Financial Performance, Islamic Banking, Full-Fledged Banks (US data).
aUSZQDIBP.how_to_use: Niche — Islamic Finance Development Indicator. US has few full-fledged Islamic banks; data is thin.

aUSZPDIBR.description: IFDI, Financial Performance Indicator, Islamic Banking, Return on Assets
aUSZPDIBR.meaning: IFDI Return on Assets, Islamic Banking.
aUSZPDIBR.how_to_use: Cross-country comparable Islamic banking metric. US presence is small.

aUSZPDIBP.meaning: IFDI Islamic Banking windows (conventional banks with Islamic products).

aUSPMMMR.how_to_use: Above 50 = expansion; below 50 = contraction. Sustained sub-50 prints (3+ months) historically correlate with recession risk. New orders is the most forward-looking sub-index; prices paid is an early inflation signal.
